title: How the symphony grew
subtitle: Haydn’s sudden chord to Mahler’s last few strings

hero.caption: A concert in London’s Hanover Square Rooms. Engraving in The Illustrated London News, 24 June 1843.

intro: At the Hanover Square Rooms in 1792, Haydn startled London with a single chord. A little over a century later, the last page of Mahler’s Ninth needs only strings, played softly.

stations.title: Haydn’s surprise
stations.text: London, 23 March 1792. At Salomon’s concert in the Hanover Square Rooms, Haydn’s new symphony had the strings play a short, plain tune. They repeat it more softly. Then the whole orchestra plays one fortissimo chord, with timpani. Haydn wrote the symphony during his first London visit. The slow movement sets its C-major tune as a series of variations. In the first variation the second violins and violas keep the melody while the first violins play semiquavers around it.

cues.text: The strings begin a short tune in C major, with a bass note at the start of each bar.
The quiet repeat ends with a single fortissimo chord from the whole orchestra, including timpani.
The first violins play semiquavers around the tune, now held by the second violins and violas.

stations.title: Mozart’s return by a different route
stations.text: Three years before Haydn’s London visit, Mozart wrote his G-minor Symphony, K. 550. It opens with a repeated figure in the violins. In the development, fragments of it pass between strings and winds, and each repetition moves into a less stable key. Mozart then brings the opening back in G minor. The recapitulation is longer than the exposition because the bridge between the themes modulates further. The second theme, first heard in B♭ major, returns in G minor, with semitone clashes in the woodwind and strings.

cues.text: Scraps of the opening violin figure pass between instruments and through changing keys.
The opening returns in G minor; the bridge between the themes is now longer.
The second theme returns in G minor; it was first heard in B♭ major.

stations.title: Mozart: five themes in combination
stations.text: Mozart wrote the Jupiter Symphony in the summer of 1788, the same summer as the G-minor. In the finale the four-note tune C–D–F–E keeps its long notes while quicker figures pass it, and one part can begin before another has finished. The return to C major is followed by further development. In the coda five themes are combined, each keeping its own rhythm as they pass between the instruments. Trumpets and timpani join the final C-major chords.

cues.text: The four-note tune returns in C major, with quicker figures moving around it.
In the coda five themes are combined, with long notes set against running figures and short replies.
Trumpets and timpani reinforce the final C-major chords as the running lines converge.

stations.title: Beethoven: a pause for an oboe
stations.text: The Fifth’s opening rhythm continues to work long after its first statement. In the development it passes between instruments and through changing keys, and the exchanges eventually shrink to isolated chords, with silence between the replies. When the opening returns at bar 248, winds and brass reinforce it. At bar 268 the orchestra stops, leaving an oboe alone in an Adagio. Later, bassoons take the call previously played by horns, and the second theme returns in C major, a minor third below its earlier E♭ major.

cues.text: The opening rhythm moves through new pitches and keys as the development begins.
Winds and strings exchange slow chords; the replies grow shorter, with rests between them.
The opening returns, with winds and brass reinforcing its short-note rhythm.
At bar 268 the orchestra stops and one oboe plays an unaccompanied Adagio.
Bassoons take the horns’ old call before the second theme returns in C major.

stations.title: Brahms’s greeting from the mountains
stations.text: In 1868 Brahms sent Clara Schumann a melody from the Bernese Alps, with the words: “High on the mountain, deep in the valley, I greet you many thousand times.” Eight years later a horn plays a version of that melody in the finale of his First Symphony, over tremolo strings; flutes then take it over. Trombones and bassoons follow with a short chorale. All this comes before the long string theme of the main Allegro. The chorale returns, played loud, in the coda.

cues.text: The long wind call is held above strings playing rapidly repeated notes.
Trombones and bassoons play a short chorale. It does not appear again until the coda.
The call dies away, and the main Allegro follows after this excerpt.

stations.title: Bruckner and the string writing
stations.text: A short repeated figure in the strings opens the scherzo of the Seventh, in A minor. Over it a trumpet plays a call and the clarinet answers; this exchange supplies much of the material for a movement built on large orchestral crescendos. Bruckner returns repeatedly to the same short figures, moves them between instruments and builds them into long crescendos. Between the loud passages the brass play quietly: trombones and tuba join in a soft chorale while the strings continue to move. Another crescendo begins before the excerpt ends. After it comes the slower trio in F major, in which quiet timpani introduce a melody for the violins.

cues.text: A short repeated figure in the strings opens the scherzo, and a trumpet call rises above it.
Brass and timpani join the strings in the first loud passage.
Trombones and tuba play softly in the quieter passage; the strings stay busy beneath them.
Winds and brass join the strings in another crescendo before the slower trio.

stations.title: Tchaikovsky’s fading basses
stations.text: In Klin on 23 February 1893, Tchaikovsky told his nephew Vladimir Davydov that the Sixth would end with “the most drawn-out Adagio”. He was delighted with the new symphony. Here, after the low-brass chorale, a melody first heard in D major returns in B minor and rises to one last climax. The orchestra then drops out until only the low strings remain, and the double basses repeat B as the texture thins. Their pulse grows softer until it is barely audible.

cues.text: The second theme returns in B minor, over the low B in the basses.
The strings play one last swell.
The remaining phrase descends towards the low strings and their repeated bass pulse.
The double basses hold a B, growing softer, as the symphony ends quietly.

stations.title: Mahler and silence in the symphony
stations.text: The last page of Mahler’s Ninth begins with muted second violins. The marking is Adagissimo, slower still. Only strings remain, and the long melodies of the finale have broken into phrases of a few notes, separated by rests. One note is held after the others stop, and another, played softly, follows it. A viola plays a small upward turn inside the last D♭-major chord.

cues.text: Adagissimo: muted second violins begin the final page, with strings alone and long rests between phrases.
The viola plays its phrase upwards inside the last D♭-major chord, and the remaining notes die away.
